requirements: Dieters can log their daily food intake by scanning barcodes of packaged foods or searching a database of common foods
Nutritionists can create personalized meal plans for clients based on their dietary goals and restrictions
Users can track their macronutrient intake and receive alerts when they exceed daily limits
Caregivers can monitor the eating habits of their dependents and receive notifications when certain foods are consumed
Chefs can create and share recipes with nutritional information and cooking instructions
Food manufacturers can upload and manage their product information, including ingredients and nutritional content
Dieters can track their progress over time and receive recommendations for improving their diet based on their eating habits
Restaurant owners can create and manage menus with nutritional information, allowing customers to make informed choices
The system must be able to handle a large volume of user-submitted food data, with an average of 10,000 new entries per day
Nutritional information must be updated at least quarterly to reflect changes in food composition and dietary guidelines
The system must be accessible on both desktop and mobile devices, with an average page load time of less than 2 seconds
User data must be protected with encryption and secure authentication, with a maximum downtime of 1 hour per month for maintenance
The system must be able to integrate with popular fitness trackers and health apps, allowing for seamless data exchange and synchronization

requirements: Nutritionists can log a patient's meal intake by selecting predefined food items from a database categorized by macronutrient content (e.g., '1 cup of cooked quinoa - 222 calories, 8g protein, 39g carbs, 4g fat').
Patients can scan a barcode on packaged food items to automatically log nutritional information (e.g., calories, sodium, sugars) into their daily intake record.
Dietitians can set personalized daily caloric and macronutrient targets for patients, with the system flagging meals that exceed or fall short of these targets.
Patients can upload photos of homemade meals, and the system uses image recognition to estimate portion sizes and approximate nutritional content for manual verification.
Caregivers (e.g., parents, spouses) can view a patient's meal history and receive alerts if the patient skips meals or exceeds daily sodium intake limits.
The system generates a weekly nutrition report for patients, summarizing trends in caloric intake, protein consumption, and micronutrient deficiencies, with comparisons to dietary guidelines.
Patients with dietary restrictions (e.g., gluten-free, vegan) can filter food databases to exclude incompatible items, and the system highlights potential allergens in meal suggestions.
Nutritionists can prescribe meal plans with specific portion sizes, and the system sends push notifications to patients at scheduled times to remind them to log their meals.
The system integrates with wearable devices (e.g., smart scales, fitness trackers) to correlate meal intake with weight trends and activity levels, providing insights into metabolic responses.
Patients can share their meal logs with healthcare providers (e.g., doctors, dietitians) via a secure link, enabling remote monitoring of dietary adherence and progress toward nutritional goals.
The system must process barcode scans and update nutritional databases within 2 seconds to ensure real-time logging accuracy for patients tracking meals during grocery shopping.
Meal photo uploads must be compressed to under 500KB to maintain system responsiveness, as patients may upload multiple images per day from mobile devices with limited bandwidth.
Nutrition reports must generate within 10 seconds of request to avoid delays in patient-doctor consultations, even when processing 12 months of historical meal data.
The system must support offline mode for patients in areas with poor connectivity, syncing logged meals and updates to the cloud once a stable connection is restored within 30 minutes.
All nutritional data must be stored with a precision of ±5% for macronutrients and ±10% for micronutrients to comply with FDA labeling accuracy standards for dietary tracking systems.
